headline: How Wi-Fi, IPs and Browsers Build the Web
tldr: A guided tour of every layer between your Wi-Fi router and the website on your screen.

mindmap.label: How the Internet Works
mindmap.note: The internet is a collaborative, globally shared network of computers that moves your data through hardware, protocols, and software to deliver websites, email, and streaming.

children.label: Getting Online Locally
children.note: Every device needs hardware and software to bridge into a local network before reaching the wider internet.

children.label: Local networks as bridges
children.note: Home Wi-Fi or a phone's cellular network links your device to the global internet.

children.label: Wi-Fi uses radio waves
children.note: Wi-Fi wirelessly transmits data between your device and a router, which connects onward to your ISP.

children.label: Routers as traffic managers
children.note: Routers forward requests to your ISP and assign local IP addresses to keep devices organized and secure.

children.label: Wired vs wireless links
children.note: Ethernet cables are typically faster and more stable; Wi-Fi and cellular offer flexibility and mobility.

children.label: Addressing and Data Movement
children.note: Devices are identified by IP addresses, and data itself travels as small reassembled packets rather than one whole file.

children.label: IP addresses identify devices
children.note: Every device gets a unique IP address, like a home address, so data knows where to go; IPv4 is common but IPv6 is growing.

children.label: Data travels as packets
children.note: Messages break into packets that can take different routes and get reassembled at the destination, making transfer fast and reliable.

children.label: TCP/IP is the foundation
children.note: TCP breaks data into packets and ensures correct delivery, while IP handles addressing and routing.

children.label: Bandwidth and latency
children.note: Bandwidth is how much data can move at once; latency (ping) is the delay per request, critical for gaming and calls.

children.label: The Backbone and ISPs
children.note: Beyond your home, high-speed cables and providers carry data across the planet.

children.label: Internet backbone
children.note: High-speed cables and powerful routers connect major cities and countries, including undersea cables and fiber optic lines.

children.label: ISPs connect you to it all
children.note: Internet service providers maintain infrastructure, manage traffic, and assign your IP address.

children.label: From Domain Name to Website
children.note: Typing a web address triggers a lookup and request chain that ends with a page rendered in your browser.

children.label: Domain names vs IP addresses
children.note: Easy-to-remember domain names map to numerical IP addresses behind the scenes.

children.label: DNS as the phone book
children.note: DNS servers translate domain names into IP addresses in milliseconds.

children.label: Request reaches the web server
children.note: The request travels through your local network, ISP, and backbone before the server responds with site data.

children.label: Web servers store site files
children.note: Servers stay online to deliver HTML, images, and scripts to browsers on request.

children.label: Building the Web Page
children.note: Three core web languages combine so the browser can turn raw data into a usable page.

children.label: Browsers render the data
children.note: The browser interprets code and manages security, cookies, and plugins for a smooth experience.

children.label: HTML structures content
children.note: HTML defines headings, paragraphs, and links as the backbone of every website.

children.label: CSS styles the page
children.note: CSS controls colors, fonts, and layout, turning plain text into a designed page.

children.label: JavaScript adds interactivity
children.note: JavaScript runs in-browser to power buttons, popups, and dynamic content.

children.label: Keeping the Internet Secure
children.note: Encryption, barriers, and good habits protect data as it moves and while it sits on your device.

children.label: HTTPS encrypts traffic
children.note: HTTPS prevents hackers from intercepting passwords or credit card numbers; look for the padlock icon.

children.label: Firewalls block bad traffic
children.note: Firewalls monitor and control network traffic as hardware or software barriers.

children.label: VPNs create secure tunnels
children.note: VPNs encrypt data, hide your IP, and let you access region-restricted content.

children.label: Malware and phishing threats
children.note: Malware harms devices or steals data; phishing tricks users into handing it over, so use security tools and check suspicious links.

children.label: Digital privacy habits
children.note: Strong passwords, two-factor authentication, and encrypted messaging apps help keep personal information safe.

children.label: What Runs On Top
children.note: Everyday internet services and technologies all rely on the layers built up earlier in the video.

children.label: Email routing
children.note: Messages travel from your device to your email server, then to the recipient's server.

children.label: Video streaming in chunks
children.note: Video is broken into chunks and buffered so you can watch before the whole file downloads.

children.label: Cloud computing
children.note: Files and apps run on remote servers, accessible from anywhere with a connection.

children.label: Social media at scale
children.note: Powerful servers and databases let platforms manage millions of users and posts.

children.label: E-commerce
children.note: Encryption and authentication protect payments and personal data during online shopping.

children.label: Search engines
children.note: Algorithms index billions of pages and rank results by relevance and quality.

children.label: Cookies and tracking
children.note: Cookies remember preferences and login status but can also be used for tracking and ads.

children.label: Mobile and IoT
children.note: 4G/5G keep phones connected on the go, while IoT connects everyday objects like thermostats and lights.

children.label: P2P networks
children.note: Devices communicate directly without a central server, powering file sharing and some cryptocurrencies.

children.label: Open source software
children.note: Freely available code powers web servers and browsers, encouraging global collaboration.

children.label: Hosting and CDNs
children.note: Hosting providers store site files while CDNs cache copies globally to cut load times.

children.label: Rules and Governance
children.note: Shared protocols and standards bodies keep a decentralized internet interoperable and fair.

children.label: Protocols set the rules
children.note: HTTP, FTP, and SMTP are common standards letting different systems work together.

children.label: Net neutrality
children.note: The principle that ISPs must treat all traffic equally, keeping the internet open and fair.

children.label: Standards bodies
children.note: Groups like ICANN, IETF, and W3C set rules for domain names, protocols, and web standards.

children.label: The internet's future
children.note: 5G, AI, and quantum computing are expected to bring faster speeds and smarter services.

cards.q: What are the two main types of IP address mentioned?
cards.a: IPv4, which is most common, and IPv6, which is becoming more important as more devices connect.
It translates human-friendly domain names into machine-readable IP addresses, acting like the internet's phone book.

cards.q: Why does the internet break data into packets?
cards.a: Packets can take different routes and be reassembled at the destination, making the internet fast and reliable even when parts are busy or down.

cards.q: What do HTML, CSS, and JavaScript each do?
cards.a: HTML structures content, CSS controls look and feel, and JavaScript adds interactivity and dynamic behavior.
It encrypts data between browser and server so hackers can't intercept passwords or credit card numbers.

cards.q: What is TCP/IP's role in internet communication?
cards.a: TCP breaks data into packets and ensures correct delivery, while IP handles addressing and routing.
The principle that all internet traffic should be treated equally, preventing ISPs from favoring certain sites or services.

cards.q: What do content delivery networks (CDNs) do?
cards.a: They store copies of website files on servers worldwide so content loads from the nearest server, cutting load times.

summary: The video walks through the internet as a layered system, starting with how a device gets online at all: Wi-Fi and routers form the local bridge between your phone or laptop and your internet service provider, with routers acting as traffic managers that assign local IP addresses and forward requests outward.

From there it explains addressing and transport — every device has a unique IP address, and data is chopped into packets that travel independently and get reassembled at the destination, riding on a physical backbone of undersea cables and fiber optic lines that ISPs help maintain and connect you to.

The heart of the video is the journey from typing a URL to seeing a page: DNS translates the domain name into an IP address, the request reaches a web server, and the response comes back as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, which the browser assembles into the page you see, all typically wrapped in HTTPS encryption and filtered by firewalls.

It then surveys the services built on top of this stack — email, streaming, cloud computing, social media, e-commerce, search engines, cookies, mobile data, IoT, VPNs, P2P networks, open source software, hosting, and CDNs — showing how the same underlying plumbing supports very different everyday uses.

Finally, it zooms out to the rules that hold it together: protocols like HTTP, FTP, and SMTP, the TCP/IP foundation, concepts like bandwidth and latency, security threats like malware and phishing, and governance principles like net neutrality enforced loosely through standards bodies like ICANN, IETF, and W3C.
moves: Check your browser for the padlock icon before entering passwords or payment info on any site
Look up whether your home router is set to IPv4, IPv6, or both
Turn on two-factor authentication for your most important accounts
Try a `ping` or traceroute to see the latency and hops to a favorite website
Review and clear cookies in your browser's privacy settings

receipts.title: IP addresses identify every device
receipts.detail: Every device gets a unique IP address that works like a home address so data can find its way, with IPv4 dominant today and IPv6 growing as more devices connect.

receipts.title: Data moves as packets, not one stream
receipts.detail: Messages and files are broken into smaller packets that can each take different routes through the network and are reassembled at the destination, keeping the internet fast even when parts are congested.

receipts.title: DNS is the internet's phone book
receipts.detail: DNS servers translate human-friendly domain names into the numerical IP addresses machines need, completing the lookup in milliseconds.

receipts.title: Three languages build every web page
receipts.detail: HTML structures content, CSS handles visual styling, and JavaScript adds interactivity — together they turn raw server data into the pages you browse.

receipts.title: HTTPS encrypts your connection
receipts.detail: HTTPS encrypts data between your browser and the web server so hackers can't intercept passwords or credit card numbers; the padlock icon signals a secure connection.

receipts.title: TCP/IP is the internet's foundation
receipts.detail: TCP breaks data into packets and guarantees correct delivery while IP handles addressing and routing, and together they make reliable global data exchange possible.

receipts.title: Bandwidth and latency shape your experience
receipts.detail: Bandwidth caps how much data can move at once, while latency (ping) is the delay per request; low latency matters most for gaming, calls, and real-time apps.

receipts.title: Malware and phishing are the main threats
receipts.detail: Malware is malicious software that harms devices or steals data, while phishing tricks people into handing over data by impersonating trusted sources.

receipts.title: Net neutrality keeps traffic equal
receipts.detail: Net neutrality is the principle that ISPs must treat all internet traffic equally, preventing them from favoring certain websites or services over others.

receipts.title: Standards bodies govern the open internet
receipts.detail: Organizations like ICANN, IETF, and W3C collaboratively set the rules for domain names, protocols, and web standards, keeping the internet open and interoperable.
